title: The Support Scope handles governance processes grounded in explicit Atlas rules, while contentious or ambiguous cases escalate to the Governance Scope
content:
A.2 opens by giving the Support Scope authority over "all routine aspects of ecosystem support, including governance process infrastructure and management, Agent support and Ecosystem Actor support." A.2.1.1.1 then draws the boundary that matters: the Support Scope "regulates routine governance processes based in the explicit rules of the Atlas," whereas "the Governance Scope governs situations in which a document is appealed or is otherwise contentious for reasons of ambiguity or conflict with other documents."

The split is by **interpretive load, not by topic**. The same governance artifact — a poll, an Atlas Edit Proposal, a change to Active Data — sits in Support while its handling is mechanical, and crosses into Governance the moment its meaning is disputed. The annotations pin down the trigger words: "ambiguity" means the language permits multiple interpretations (A.2.1.1.1.0.3.1), "contentious" means there is disagreement over interpretation, application, or validity (A.2.1.1.1.0.3.2), and "document is appealed" means a formal request has reached the Core Facilitator (A.2.1.1.1.0.3.3).

Why this is load-bearing: it lets the high-volume machinery of governance — Aligned Delegate processes, the Weekly and Monthly Governance Cycles — run under a Scope optimized for throughput and rule-following, without contaminating it with judgment calls. Judgment is concentrated elsewhere, where a different (and slower) standard of care can apply.

The trade-off is that the escalation trigger is itself a judgment. Whoever decides that language is "ambiguous" or a matter "contentious" effectively decides which Scope's rules govern, so the routing decision becomes a quiet locus of power.
description: The dividing line is interpretive difficulty, not subject matter: appeal, ambiguity, or conflict with another document moves a process out of Support and into Governance.
